uncited: Parallelism and Distribution addresses the computational bottleneck of volume rendering by distributing ray casting, compositing, or voxel processing tasks across multiple processors, threads, or networked nodes to achieve real-time or near-real-time frame rates.

It differs from sibling acceleration techniques like [Early Termination and Probabilistic Path Control](1791-early-termination-and-probabilistic-path-control.md) or [Visibility Culling](6226-visibility-culling.md), which optimize the work per ray, by instead increasing the total throughput of the rendering pipeline through hardware or cluster-level concurrency.
The core mechanism of this family is the decomposition of the rendering problem into independent or semi-independent units of work that can be executed concurrently.
**Spatial Decomposition:** Dividing the image plane (e.g., by rows or tiles) or the volume space (e.g., by X-axis slices or bricks) among processing units.
**Task Scheduling:** Using a central manager or distributed scheduler to assign tasks (such as ray segments or voxel blocks) to available workers, often handling load balancing dynamically.

**Communication Overhead Management:** Minimizing data transfer between processors, either by keeping data local (shared memory) or by optimizing network traffic (e.g., overlapping communication with computation).

Mathematically, if $N$ is the total number of rays or voxels and $P$ is the number of processors, the ideal speedup is $S = N/P$, subject to Amdahl's Law constraints imposed by serial portions of the code (e.g., final image assembly or synchronization).
Parallel volume rendering has evolved from early shared-memory multi-threading approaches to distributed cluster rendering.
